title: Why I Stay an IC
intro: His case for why senior UX researchers don't need a management title to lead.

learn.title: What companies actually value
learn.text:
A lot of companies say they value research. What they really value is **confidence**.

If you're not careful, research becomes the thing that supplies it: “go test this”, or worse, “get a quick user quote to support this deck”.

The context is the end of what he calls the **“easy money era”** of the early 2020s, when teams could build freely, fail often and try again.

try.q: What does Calabro say companies really value, as opposed to what they say?
options: Confidence
Speed of delivery above all
Evidence
User satisfaction
try.explain: Which is how research gets reduced to supplying it after the decision.

learn.title: The “customer representative” trap
learn.text:
Under delivery pressure, PMs shortcut user data — summarising Slack messages, speaking for the customer from memory.

It isn't that they're anti-user. They're moving fast, and real research seems slow **unless someone shows them a better way**.

A senior IC is positioned to do exactly that:

• Sit in roadmap planning and say “before we commit, can I show you what users are actually trying to do?”
• Reframe a feature spec into a hypothesis testable **this week** instead of next quarter
• Take a vague business goal and show how it maps — or doesn't — to actual behaviour
• Work **across teams**, not just within a reporting structure

try.q: Why do PMs end up acting as the customer representative?
options: Research seems slow unless shown a better way
They distrust research methods
They are measured on user satisfaction
They have been trained to do it
try.explain: It's delivery pressure, not hostility to users.

learn.title: Tactics that work
learn.text:
**Ask reframing questions** — change what the team is deciding, not just what gets tested.
**Think outcomes over artifacts** — the deck isn't the deliverable; the decision is.
**Get good at moving faster** — speed is what buys you the seat.

He also reframes research as a way to **de-risk investment**: not just user-centred, but cost-conscious.

And his rule of thumb: *“if you ever find yourself talking to non-UXers about cognitive load, you're doing it wrong.”*

try.q: What is his rule of thumb about talking to non-UXers?
options: Don't talk to them about cognitive load
Always bring a working prototype to the meeting
Lead with the method
Translate findings into personas
try.explain: Speak in their terms — risk, cost, outcomes.

test.q: How does a senior IC reframe research for stakeholders?
options: As a way to de-risk investment
As a quality gate before release
As a service with a fixed turnaround
As a design input

test.q: What happens to research when a company values confidence above all?
options: It gets used to justify decisions already made
It gets more budget than it needs
As a service with a fixed turnaround time
It moves earlier in the process
test.explain: “Go test this” or “get a quick user quote to support this deck”.

test.q: Which tactic is on his list?
options: Think outcomes over artifacts
Publish a quarterly research report
Run more studies per sprint
Train PMs in research methods
test.explain: Along with asking reframing questions and moving faster.

test.q: What does “work across teams” mean here?
options: Influence beyond your reporting structure
Join several squads at once
Share findings in a central repository
Rotate between product areas every quarter
test.explain: An IC's reach isn't bounded by the org chart.

options: The early 2020s, when teams could build and fail freely
The period before UX had job titles
The boom in UX bootcamps
The years before AI tooling
test.explain: The context for why research is under pressure now.
